intro: Almost everyone believes the same thing about a remote career: grind three years, and three years of experience will quietly turn into a higher rate. It will not. Time is not the variable. This page lets you watch that play out, side by side with the person who chose differently.

hero.kicker: Career simulator · 36 months · a model, not a promise
hero.titleLine2: is not three years of leverage.
hero.lead: Set your craft, your AI, and what you sell. The simulator draws two lines over 36 months: the generic task-taker, and you. The gap between them is the entire lesson, and if there is no gap, that is the lesson too.

banner.title: Read this before you read a single number.
banner.body: This is a MODEL. It is not a prediction, a forecast, a promise, or an offer. Nobody can tell you what you will earn, not us, not a salary guide, not a coach. What a model can honestly do is show you the shape of a decision: which choices bend the line, and which ones only feel like they do. Every figure below means 'roughly, directionally, if the model is right'. Treat it as a teaching instrument, never as a plan for your rent.
banner.oneLine: A model, not a prediction. Every figure below means "roughly, directionally, if the model is right"; never plan your rent on it.

dataHonesty.title: Why nobody has an honest chart of Philippine freelance rates, including us
dataHonesty.body: There is no authoritative public dataset of Philippine freelancer rates by seniority. None exists. Every "2026 salary guide" you will find is published by a staffing agency, an outsourcing firm, or a training company: pages with no disclosed methodology, no sample size, and a direct commercial reason to skew the number, up if they sell training, down if they sell cheap labour. The base rates in this simulator are the convergent directional picture across several of those sources. That makes them vendor-grade, not survey-grade, and we will not dress them up as anything better.
dataHonesty.disagreement: How soft is that ground? Two vendor guides put the same entry-level bookkeeping role at $5–6/hr and $10–12/hr, a 2x disagreement about one job in one year. The Salary Guide shows the same problem with an even wider spread on support roles.

controls.title: Your six inputs
controls.lead: Only one of these sets your floor. The other five are multipliers, and a multiplier on a small number is still a small number.

craft.help: This is the only input that sets your base rate. Everything after it just multiplies whatever this gives you.

options.label: No craft yet
options.desc: General task work: inbox, data entry, scheduling, whatever gets handed over. Anyone with a laptop can be swapped in for you tomorrow.

options.label: Building one
options.desc: You picked a specialisation and you are deliberately getting good at it. Not there yet, but the direction is real.

options.label: Specialised
options.desc: Bookkeeping, ecommerce ops, automation, medical ops, paid media, dev. You are the person they call when it breaks.

ai.help: AI multiplies a craft. Look closely at what it does to your line when there is no craft under it.

options.label: I don't use it
options.desc: Honest position. Nobody is paying a premium for the absence of it either.

options.label: I use ChatGPT to work faster
options.desc: You draft faster and reply faster. So does every other person with a browser and a no-cost account.

options.label: I build AI into the delivery
options.desc: Automations, AI QA passes, AI-assisted ops, that you designed, that you own, and that you can fix at 2am when they break.

ownership.help: Hours have a ceiling: there are only so many of them, and everyone's are the same length.

options.label: Hours and tasks
options.desc: You do what you're told and bill the time. Someone else decides whether it worked.

options.label: An outcome, end to end
options.desc: You own the result: the books close, the ads perform, the pipeline runs. Nobody hands you a checklist.

hours.help: Hours billed, not hours sat at the desk. The two are famously not the same number.

options.label: 10 hrs
options.desc: Side hustle, on top of a day job.

language.help: English is a national baseline here, not an edge. Treating it as a superpower is how a lot of people end up competing on price.

options.label: English
options.desc: The floor everyone in this market already stands on.

options.label: English + Japanese / Korean / Mandarin
options.desc: A thinner pool of competitors, which is the only reason a rate moves.

clients.help: Same work. Different budget on the other end of the call.

options.label: US / AU / UK clients
options.desc: The reference case. The base rates above already assume this, it is not a bonus.

options.label: Philippine clients
options.desc: Same work you'd do for a foreign client, priced against local budgets.

chart.title: 36 months, two lives
chart.lead: Both lines are monthly take-home after the unpaid-time tax below. Same hours. Same client market. The only difference is what the person chose to become.
chart.riskBandNote: The shaded band under your line is not a forecast, it is a warning: roughly one in three cloudworkers has experienced outright non-payment; the full numbers are in the reality tax below. Your line is not a floor.
chart.tableCaption: The same two trajectories as a table, monthly take-home in USD, after the unpaid-time tax.

results.title: What the model says
results.milestoneLabel: Monthly take-home, after the unpaid-time tax
results.rangeNote: Vendor-grade base range for this craft

fx.label: Assumed exchange rate
fx.note: This is an assumption, and FX moves. Change it to whatever today's rate is, the peso figures update live. We default to ₱{fx}, the BSP rate sampled in {sampled}, so check it against today's number before you trust it.

multipliers.title: Every multiplier, and where it came from
multipliers.lead: One of these is sourced. The rest are ours. We are not going to blur the difference, that blurring is exactly how salary-guide pages get built.
multipliers.baseLabel: Base hourly rate, from your craft
multipliers.baseNote: Vendor-grade and directional. This number, and only this number, is set by your craft. Read the honesty section above before you trust it to two decimal places.

ai-none.label: AI, not used
ai-none.note: No premium, no penalty. The market does not pay you for abstaining.

ai-user.label: AI, you use ChatGPT
ai-user.note: Being faster at typing is not a differentiator. Everyone has the same no-cost account. We give it a rounding error, because that is what it is worth.

ai-augmented-deep.label: AI, built into a deep craft
ai-augmented-deep.note: This is the one number on the page with real research behind it. Upwork reports freelancers doing AI work earn 34% more per hour, so the multiplier is ×1.34, a vendor-reported figure, not an independently audited one, but the nuance matters more than the headline: the callout below shows where that premium lands.

ai-augmented-building.label: AI, built into a craft you're still learning
ai-augmented-building.note: You get a partial version of the AI premium, because you have a partial craft. The multiplier is honest about that: half-built expertise, half-sized premium.

ai-augmented-none.label: AI, built on top of no craft
ai-augmented-none.note: ×1.0. No premium. This is not a bug: see the callout below. AI multiplies a craft. There is nothing here for it to multiply.

ownership-tasks.label: Ownership, you bill hours
ownership-tasks.note: The reference case. Your ceiling is the clock, and the clock does not get longer.

ownership-outcomes.label: Ownership, you own an outcome
ownership-outcomes.note: Our number, but grounded: Upwork's Future Workforce Index 2025 found the companies with the highest revenue growth are far likelier to buy managed services (50%) and human+AI collaboration (41%). They are buying a delivered result, not a seat-hour. The +25% is our estimate of what that is worth to you.

language-english.label: Language, English
language-english.note: ×1.0. English is the baseline in this market, not an edge.

language-second.label: Language, a second language
language-second.note: Our number, flagged as such. The logic is competition, not merit: a thinner pool moves a rate. And a reality check on the English assumption, the Philippines ranks 28th of 123 on the EF EPI 2025, having fallen six places.

clients-foreign.label: Clients, US / AU / UK
clients-foreign.note: ×1.0. The base rates already assume this market. It is the reference case, not a bonus.

clients-local.label: Clients, Philippine
clients-local.note: Our number. Same work, local budgets. It is not a judgement on local clients, it is arithmetic about what they can pay.

axios-ai.label: Axios, AI, vibe coding and the Upwork premium

aiCallout.title: You layered AI on top of nothing. The model gives you nothing.
aiCallout.body: You selected "I build AI into the delivery" with no craft underneath it, and your AI multiplier came out at ×1.0, no premium at all. That is deliberate, and it is the most important line of code on this page. The AI premium is real and it is sourced. It just does not belong to you yet.
aiCallout.quote: If you were a traditional machine learning expert, and now you're augmenting that work with generative AI, you're seeing such a great premium.
aiCallout.attribution: Kelly Monahan, Managing Director, Upwork Research Institute
aiCallout.closer: Read that again slowly. The premium accrues to the person who already had the expertise. AI is a multiplier, and a multiplier needs something to multiply. Go pick a craft, get good at it, and then come back and set this to "deep", the same AI skill you already have will be worth a great deal more.

realityTax.title: The reality tax, applied to every number on this page

unpaid.title: ×0.75 · the unpaid quarter
unpaid.body: The ILO found online workers spend roughly 20 unpaid minutes for every paid hour, hunting for work, doing unpaid tests, vetting clients who ghost. About a quarter of your working time earns nothing. Every figure in this simulator is multiplied by 0.75 for it. That figure comes from a 2015–2017 ILO survey, the most recent of its kind, so today's platforms may look better or worse than this snapshot. And a number worth sitting with: average hourly earnings in Asia-Pacific, once you count the unpaid time, came to $2.22/hr.

source.label: ILO, Digital labour platforms and the future of work (2018), surveys 2015–2017

nonPayment.title: 31% · the people who never got paid at all
nonPayment.body: Fairwork's Cloudwork Ratings 2025 (Oxford Internet Institute; 750+ workers across 100 countries) found 31% of cloudworkers had experienced non-payment and 38% had experienced late payment. That is not a deduction we can average into a line, it is a risk you either survive or don't. So it is drawn as a band under your line instead. Roughly one in three people get stiffed at least once. Contracts, escrow, and deposits are not paranoia; they are the job.

verdicts.label: In three years, this path pays you roughly what it pays you today.
verdicts.body: Look at your line. It climbs for a quarter, and then it is a horizontal ruler for the next thirty-three months. That is not a glitch, it is what a career looks like when the thing you sell is availability. There is nothing underneath to compound, so nothing compounds. You will be busier in month 36 than in month 6. You will not be richer.

verdicts.label: It moves. Barely. Mostly it is still time you are selling.
verdicts.body: Your line lifts a little over three years, but it does not bend, and a line that does not bend is a line that never escapes. Whatever premium you have picked up here is a nice adjustment to a small number. Look at which input is doing the lifting, then look at your craft. That is where the bend has to come from.

verdicts.label: This one bends. You are building something that pays you back.
verdicts.body: There is real separation from the generic line now, and it is widening rather than settling. Notice the shape: the ramp is slow and then it steepens, because craft is slow and then it compounds. The temptation at month 8, when the line is still low and the work is hard, is to conclude it isn't working. That is precisely the month most people quit.

verdicts.label: This is the divergence. Same 36 months, a different life.
verdicts.body: Your line and the generic line started in the same place with the same hours, and they no longer live in the same world. Nothing about that gap is time. Every dollar of it came from a decision: to specialise, to build AI into the delivery instead of just typing into it, to own a result rather than bill an hour. This is what leverage looks like on a chart, and the model is still the optimistic version, because it cannot see the client who doesn't pay.

gapNote.same: At month 36 you and the generic task-taker are earning roughly the same money. Three years, same number. That is the whole point of this page.
gapNote.diverged: At month 36 your path earns about {x}× what the generic task-taker earns, on the same hours, in the same market. Not one hour of that gap was bought with time.

outro.title: The numbers were never the hard part.
outro.body: The hard part is that the highest line on this chart belongs to someone who spent 30 months being worse than they wanted to be, at one specific thing, on purpose. There is no version of this where the line bends and the craft doesn't. Get the real market data, then pick the thing.
